abstract.p: The rhizome of Smilax glabra Roxb., known as Smilacis glabrae Rhizoma, is extensively used in Traditional Chinese Medicine for relieving dampness and other health issues. The growth patterns and geographical distribution of S. glabra are significantly influenced by ecological conditions. This study used the maximum entropy (MaxEnt) modeling approach in combination with the geographic information system (GIS) software (ArcMap) to evaluate and predict the influence of climate change on the geographical distribution of S. glabra. The potential suitable habitats under two greenhouse gas emission scenarios (SSP126 and SSP370) were forecast for two future timeframes (2041–2060 and 2061–2080) by analyzing species occurrence records and environmental factors. Jackknife method was employed to assess the significance of environmental variables, and those contributing ≥ 1.0% to the model were considered as major driving factors. S. glabra is widely distributed in the southern provincial regions of the Yangtze River Basin in China. Currently, the suitable habitat covers 1,755,900 km2. In the predicted future climate scenarios, the suitable habitat area is projected to extend to a maximum of 1,915,400 km2. The distribution of S. glabra is significantly influenced by rainfall, daily temperature variation, and soil clay composition. Moreover, under both the projected climate scenarios, the core of suitable habitats for S. glabra were predicted to migrate southward. Overall, our findings offer a scientific basis for developing conservation approaches and optimize their spatial distribution management of the genetic sources of S. glabra.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Smilax Glabrae Rhizoma refers to the dried rhizome of Smilax glabra Roxb., a plant species belonging to the Smilacaceae family. It is neutral in nature, has a sweet and mild taste1. S. glabra contains a variety of bioactive compounds and is employed in the treatment of multiple diseases in clinical practice2,3. The market demand for S. glabra has surged because of its high medicinal value and status as a typical medicinal and edible plant, thereby increasing the market prices upward and generating significant economic benefits4. Currently, the wild resources of Smilax glabra (Tufuling) are characterized by an overall decline in reserves, limited distribution areas, and dual pressures from over-harvesting and ecological environmental changes. Historically, wild S. glabra was widely distributed across multiple southern provinces of China, including Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi, Jiangxi, Hunan, Hubei, Sichuan, and Guizhou. However, in recent years, the quantity of wild resources has significantly decreased. Due to ecological changes and long-term harvesting, the actual yield of wild resources has dropped from hundreds of thousands of tons in the last century to tens of thousands of tons at present. In response to resource depletion, relevant authorities have strengthened conservation measures, including increased scientific research investment, policy support, and market regulation. Examples include initiatives for germplasm resource conservation and the promotion of techniques such as crop rotation.

The quality of medicinal herbs is based on the content of their active pharmaceutical ingredient and is closely associated with the geographical origin of wild resources5–7. The ideal production areas are typically regions suitable for the growth of the medicinal plant. Medicinal herbs are often cultivated in multiple regions, but their quality varies according to habitat8. Furthermore, quality of the same medicinal herb can differ slightly even within the same region because of variations in ecological factors9. Therefore, studying how ecological factors influence the quality of medicinal herbs can guide their cultivation, improve their overall quality, and ensure the safety and efficacy of medicinal products from the source.

Climate change can cause significant shifts in the geographical range and suitability of growing environments for the medicinal plants10. For example, an increase in annual average temperature in the future is projected to cause the major distribution areas of three Fritillaria species to shift either southward or northward within Sichuan Province11. Another study found that historical warming and excessive precipitation may cause a northeastward shift in the production area of Astragalus membranaceus12. In Gentiana macrophylla, active pharmaceutical ingredients such as gentiopicroside, loganic acid and swertiamarin show significant positive or negative correlations with annual precipitation, indicating a strong influence of precipitation on its quality13. Soil is another critical ecological factor that determines the quality of medicinal herbs because it serves as the primary source of nutrients for their growth14. Soil organic matter and iron content are the dominant soil factors contributing to regional variations in the saikosaponin levels of Bupleurum chinense. Therefore, agricultural practices such as higher soil organic matter and application of iron fertilizers are used to improve saikosaponin content in B. chinense15. As a perennial medicinal plant with specific habitat requirements, environmental factors such as temperature, precipitation, and soil may similarly influence both the distribution of suitable habitats for S. glabra and the content of its medicinal active compounds. Therefore, to ensure a high quality of medicinal materials from S. glabra, it is important to understand the current geographical distribution of growing areas in China and predict potential shifts in suitable growing areas under future climate conditions based on ecological factors.

Species Distribution Models (SDMs) are statistical relationships between species occurrences and environmental data to predict potential species distribution and simulate the potential risks caused by environmental changes based on the distribution trends16. Currently, among the major SDMs and software used for such analyses, MaxEnt modeling is widely applied due to its ability to efficiently evaluate small sample sizes, superior predictive performance, as well as stable and reliable results17–19. This method has been widely demonstrated to exhibit high predictive robustness and accuracy when sample sizes are small and no true “absence” records are available20–23. In contrast, although ensemble machine learning methods such as BRT show strong overall predictive performance, their effectiveness with limited presence-only data depends more heavily on intricate parameter tuning and adequate background point sampling. ArcGIS has extensive abilities to handle complex spatial datasets and support the entire workflow from data collection to final output through its extensive modules and toolkits24–26. In this study, we integrated MaxEnt modeling with the ArcGIS software to identify the major environmental factors, influencing various climatic, topographic, and soil variables, that influence the distribution of S. glabra, based on its current distribution data. Furthermore, this study selected the SSP126 and SSP370 scenarios to represent two differentiated futures, ranging from stringent mitigation to limited mitigation. For each scenario, changes in the potentially suitable areas and shifts in the distribution centroid of Smilax glabra were projected for the periods 2041–2060 and 2061–2080, respectively. This approach aims to assess the response range of S. glabra habitats under both optimal and relatively challenging climatic conditions, thereby providing a reference for the development of climate-resilient conservation strategies.

sec.title: Collection and processing of geographic distribution data
sec.p:
The geographic distribution data for Smilax glabra Roxb. was obtained from the Chinese Virtual Herbarium (https://www.cvh.ac.cn/) and the National Specimen Information Infrastructure of China (http://www.nsii.org.cn/). The corresponding latitude and longitude coordinates were retrieved from the Baidu Maps (https://map.baidu.com/). To ensure temporal consistency with the modern climate data, we retained only occurrence records dated from the year 2000 onwards. Initially, 205 occurrence points were obtained after removing duplicate coordinates and filtering our records of specimen collections dated prior to the twenty-first century. To reduce sampling bias, these coordinates were subjected to spatial filtering using the "Spatial Rarefy Occurrence Data for SDMs" tool in ArcGIS Desktop 10.8 (https://www.esri.com/). Then, 184 spatially independent occurrence points were retained for subsequent analysis by setting the thinning parameter to a resolution of 20 km27,28. Based on these records, the spatial distribution of S. glabra in China is shown in Fig. 1.Fig. 1
Spatial distribution of Smilax glabra across China. The red dots represent the recorded presence coordinates for S. glabra.

sec.title: Collection and processing of environmental variables
sec.p: Previous studies have demonstrated that factors such as soil, climate, and precipitation significantly affect the growth and quality of medicinal herbs29. S. glabra thrives in warm and humid climates but exhibits low tolerance to cold temperatures. Its optimal growth occurs in regions with an annual average temperature of 16–23 °C, but it can tolerate temperatures up to -5 °C; moreover, precipitation is a critical determining factor for its growth30. Therefore, these factors were incorporated into the MaxEnt model. Based on the BCC-CSM2-MR model for the current and future climate scenarios, two contrasting future pathways SSP126 and SSP370, were selected to project the bioclimatic and precipitation data in the 2050s (2041–2060) and 2070s (2061–2080). The climate data used in this study were sourced from the WorldClim database (https://worldclim.org/). Soil-related data was sourced from the Harmonized World Soil Database (HWSD) (https://www.fao.org/soils-portal/data-hub/soil-maps-and-databases/harmonized-world-soil-database-v12/en/). A provincial administrative map of China at a 1: 4,000,000 scale was downloaded from the National Fundamental Geographic Information System (http://nfgis.nsdi.gov.cn) and served as the base map for this analysis. Elevation data was derived from the Geospatial Data Cloud pltform (http://www.gscloud.cn/) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and slope/aspect data was extracted using the Spatial Analyst tool in ArcMap 10.8. This study used 40 environmental variables within China and was formatted using the WGS 1984 geographic coordinate system. These datasets were suitable for MaxEnt modeling.

The selection of climatic variables is a critical step for constructing and evaluating ecological niche models because Spatial autocorrelation between the environmental variables can compromise the accuracy of model predictions31. Therefore, this study screened environmental variables to optimize the model and mitigate the impact of overfitting caused by variable redundancy32. First, the 184 species occurrence records and 40 environmental variables were imported into MaxEnt for a preliminary simulation to calculate the contribution rate of each variable. Variables with a contribution rate > 1% were retained for further analysis. Subsequently, these selected variables and the occurrence data were loaded into ArcMap 10.8. Using the “Sample” tool, the variable values at each occurrence point were extracted and exported to IBM SPSS Statistics 27.0 (https://www.ibm.com/cn-zh/products/spss) software for bivariate Pearson correlation analysis. A threshold of |r|≥ 0.8 was set to indicate high correlation31. For pairs of variables identified as highly correlated, the variable with the higher contribution rate from the preliminary simulation was retained. This screening process aims to minimize multicollinearity among variables, thereby reducing the risk of model overfitting and ensuring that the variables ultimately included in the model carry relatively independent ecological information. This screening principle was applied equally to all variable types, including climatic, precipitation, soil, and topographic factors. Through this procedure, 13 environmental variables were ultimately selected for the formal simulation (Table 1). sec.title: MaxEnt model parameterization and calibration
sec.p: Open MaxEnt 3.4.3 (https://biodiversityinformatics.amnh.org/open_source/maxent/), the longitude and latitude coordinates of S. glabra in CSV format were imported into “samples” and the filtered environmental variables in ASCII format were loaded into “environmental layers”. Then, we selected the “Create response curves” and “Do jackknife to measure variable importance” options. In the parameter settings, we enabled the “Random seed” and “Write plot data” options. A random subset of 75% of the S. glabra occurrence data was used for model training. The remaining 25% of data was reserved for model validation. The cross-validation method (“Crossvalidate”) was selected as the replication type and the number of repetitions were set to 10. The random background points were set at 10,000. The default settings were selected for other parameters.

sec.title: Model performance evaluation
sec.p: The MaxEnt model results were evaluated the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. In the ROC curves, x-axis corresponds to 1-specificity, which quantifies the false positive rate (FPR) or the likelihood of erroneously predicting the presence of a species in areas where it is truly absent. The y-axis represents sensitivity or the true positive rate (TPR), which reflects correct predictions of the presence of a species in actual distribution areas33. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC) value, which represents the probability of ranking a randomly chosen positive instance higher than a randomly chosen negative instance by the model. Therefore, higher AUC values indicate superior predictive performace of the model34. Based on Swets’ classification system35, predictive power of a model based on the AUC values is interpreted as follows: 0.5–0.6 (no predictive power); 0.6–0.7 (poor); 0.7–0.8 (good); and 0.9–1.0 (excellent). Considering the potential limitations of relying solely on the AUC metric, particularly the risk of overestimation when the background extent (set as the entire territory of China in this study) is large36, we further introduced the True Skill Statistic (TSS) for comprehensive evaluation. The TSS ranges from -1 to 1, with higher values indicating better predictive performance of the model. TSS measures a model’s ability to distinguish suitable from unsuitable habitats by comprehensively considering both sensitivity and specificity, calculated as TSS = sensitivity + specificity-1. This metric is insensitive to class imbalance problems and is therefore commonly used in species distribution modeling as a supplementary evaluation tool alongside the ROC curve37. The TSS assessment criteria are divided into four levels: excellent (0.85–1.0), good (0.70–0.85), fair (0.55–0.70), and poor (0.00–0.55)38. Additionally, we calculated the omission rate for the test dataset. This calculation was based on the logistic threshold of maximum training sensitivity plus specificity, which is a threshold that aims to balance the model’s ability to discriminate between presence and background points39.

sec.title: Classification of potential habitat suitability
sec.p: To further investigate changes in the suitable habitat areas of S. glabra under current and multiple future scenarios, ArcGIS 10.8 was used to delineate and visualize the species’ suitable distribution regions. The average results of the MaxEnt model in ASC format were imported into ArcGIS, and the maximum test sensitivity plus specificity logistic threshold was applied to define the suitable habitat areas for S. glabra. Using the natural breaks method, the potentially suitable areas were classified into four levels: unsuitable (0–0.1216), generally suitable (0.1216–0.36), moderately suitable (0.36–0.63), and highly suitable (0.63–1).

sec.title: Accuracy evaluation of the MaxEnt model
sec.p:
MaxEnt model for S. glabra achieved an AUC value of 0.935 (Fig. 2) and a TSS of 0.779 for the current period (Table 2). Furthermore, future projections (2041–2060 and 2061–2080) for the SSP126 and SSP370 scenarios also demonstrated mean AUC values above 0.9 and TSS values above 0.7 (Table 2). Additionally, under the current climatic scenario, the model demonstrates an omission rate of 6.58% on the test set, with close agreement between the omission rates of the test and training samples and the predicted omission rate (Supplementary Fig. 1). These comprehensive evaluation metrics indicate that the constructed MaxEnt model possesses good predictive performance and robustness, reduces the risk of unreliable results due to overfitting, and supports the ecological inferences derived from the subsequent analysis of environmental variable contribution rates.Fig. 2

sec.title: Correlation between critical environmental variables and geographic distribution of S. glabra
sec.p:
The influence and limiting effects of 13 environmental variables on the distribution of S. glabra habitats across mainland China were comprehensively evaluated based on the contribution rates and permutation importance values (Table 1), as well as the jackknife test results (Fig. 3). The top three environmental variables ranked by the contribution rate were mean precipitation of November (prec_11, 39.7%), precipitation of wettest quarter (bio_17, 20%), and mean precipitation of May (prec_05, 16.6%). In terms of permutation importance, the three most significant variables were mean precipitation of June (prec_06, 20.2%), mean diurnal temperature range (bio_2, 14.1%), and mean precipitation of November (prec_11, 13.5%). Higher permutation importance values indicate stronger model dependence of the model on the corresponding variable. The jackknife test results (Fig. 3) demonstrated that the mean precipitation of June (prec_06), May (prec_05), and November (prec_11) were the most influential variables. This suggested that these key precipitation-related parameters provide unique information that can significantly impact the training gain values.Fig. 3
Jackknife evaluation of the importance of distinct variables for modeling the habitat of S. glabra habitat. The analysis compares three scenarios: (1) blue bars—models using only the specified variable; (2) green bars—models excluding the target variable; (3) red bars—models incorporating all environmental variables.

The analysis revealed that the mean precipitation of November(prec_11), mean precipitation of June (prec_06), mean precipitation of May (prec_05), and precipitation of the wettest quarter (bio_17) exerted the strongest influence on the growth and distribution of S. glabra. Secondary influencing factors included mean precipitation of September and October (prec_9, prec_10), mean diurnal temperature range (bio_2), minimum temperature of the coldest month (bio_7), and temperature seasonality (bio_4). Mean temperature of the warmest quarter (bio_10), clay content (clay), and slope also exhibited measurable effects, but the impact of available soil water content (class) was less significant than these variables. Based on these findings, response curves were generated to evaluate the relationship between the four most influential environmental variables and the survival probability of S. glabra (Fig. 4). We selected the variables for which the logistic output value exceeds 0.5, indicating that the corresponding environmental factor values are conducive to plant growth. The results demonstrated significant effects of precipitation with the following optimal ranges: 58–90 mm for November, 170–500 mm for May, and 200–510 mm for June (mean precipitation values). The most favorable precipitation during the wettest quarter ranged between 120 and 450 mm.Fig. 4
Response curves for the key environmental variables. (A) Average precipitation in November; (B) Average precipitation in May; (C) Average precipitation in June; (D) Precipitation in the wettest quarter.

sec.title: Potentially suitable habitats of S. glabra across varied climate scenarios
Potentially suitable habitats under current climate conditions
sec.p:
In the current climatic conditions (Fig. 5), the total area of potentially suitable habitats for S. glabra is 1,755,900 km2, which represents 18.29% of China’s total land area. These habitats are primarily distributed across southern Chinese provinces, including Hunan, Hubei, Anhui, Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Guangdong, Guangxi, Fujian, Guizhou, and Yunnan, and partly distributed across Chongqing, Sichuan, Hainan, and Taiwan.Fig. 5
Distribution of suitable growing areas for S. glabra in China. White indicates unsuitable area; red indicates highly suitable area.

The highly suitable habitat area spans 356,500 km2 (3.71% of China’s land area) and is concentrated in western and southern Hunan, northern Guangxi, eastern Guizhou, and southern Chongqing, as well as in clusters across southern Anhui, northern Jiangxi, western Zhejiang, and northern Fujian. Highly suitable habitats were also found dispersed in southeastern Hubei, eastern Hunan, northern and southern Guangdong, southern Guangxi, western and southern Yunnan, and northern Taiwan. Moderately suitable habitats exhibit a continuous distribution pattern and cover an area spanning 720,300 km2 (7.50% of China’s land area), including the entire territories of Hunan, Guangdong, Guangxi, and Guizhou, and additional areas in southern Anhui, western Zhejiang, central and northern Jiangxi, northern Fujian, southeastern and southwestern Hubei, southern Chongqing, southeastern Sichuan, western and southern Yunnan, and Taiwan. Low-suitability habitats display a fragmented distribution pattern and cover an area of 679,100 km2 (7.07% of China’s land area), including southern Hubei, southern Anhui, eastern Zhejiang, southern Fujian, southern Jiangxi, northeastern Guangdong, central Guangxi, eastern Yunnan, eastern Sichuan, northern Chongqing, and Hainan.

sec.title: Potential distribution and area changes of S. glabra under future climatic conditions
sec.p:
The SSP126 and SSP370 greenhouse gas emission scenarios from the BCC_CSM atmospheric circulation model were used to predict the future distribution of habitats for S. glabra in two future periods (2041–2060 and 2061–2080) and four future prediction models were identified (Fig. 6). In the SSP126 scenario for 2041–2060, the total potentially suitable habitat area for S. glabra was projected to be 1,893,600 km2, accounting for 19.73% of China’s total land area. This represents an expansion of 137,700 km2 compared to the suitable habitat area under current climatic conditions. The habitat remained distributed across southern Chinese provinces, including Hunan, Hubei, Anhui, Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Guangdong, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, Fujian, Guizhou, and Yunnan, as well as smaller distributions in Chongqing, Sichuan, Jiangsu, and Taiwan (Fig. 6A). The high-suitability area was estimated to be 377,200 km2 (3.93% of China’s land area) and represented an increase of 20,700 km2 compared to the current high-suitability area. It exhibited a discontinuous distribution pattern and was primarily located in the northern and southwestern parts of Hunan, southwestern Hubei, central and northern Guizhou, southeastern Chongqing, southern Anhui, northern Jiangxi, western and southern Guangxi, and central and southern Yunnan. The moderate-suitability area was estimated to be 662,700 km2 (6.90% of China’s land area) and represented a decline of 57,600 km2 from the current area. It was distributed across central and southern Hunan, central and northern Jiangxi, southern Anhui, western and eastern Zhejiang, southeastern Fujian, southern Guangdong, northwestern and southern Guangxi, central Yunnan, southwestern Chongqing, southeastern Sichuan, and nearly the entire Guizhou province. The low-suitability area was estimated to be 853,700 km2 (8.89% of China’s land area) and represent an increase of 174,600 km2 over the current area. For the same period (2041–2060) under the SSP370 scenario (Fig. 6C), the areas of high- suitability, moderate- suitability, and low-suitability habitats for S. glabra were 397,100 km2, 631,100 km2, and 897,200 km2, respectively. The high-suitability area under the SSP370 scenario increased by 19,900 km2 compared to the SSP126 scenario for 2041–2060 period and was increased by 40,600 km2 compared to the current climatic conditions.Fig. 6
Projected distribution patterns of suitable habitats for S. glabra under future climate scenarios. (A) SSP126 (2041–2060); (B) SSP126 (2061–2080); (C) SSP370 (2041–2060); (D) SSP370 (2061–2080).

Under the SSP126 and SSP370 greenhouse gas emission scenarios, the total suitable habitat area for S. glabra in the 2061–2080 period was projected to be 1,915,400 km2 and 1,795,300 km2, respectively (Fig. 6B, D). This represents an increase of 159,500 km2 and 39,400 km2 compared to the total suitable habitat area under the current climatic conditions. The high-suitability areas in this period for the two scenarios were estimated to be 552,600 km2 and 269,500 km2, respectively. This exhibited an initial expansion followed by contraction. In the SSP126 scenario, the high-suitability area was projected to progressively expand, and the moderate-suitability area was projected to gradually decrease over time. The low-suitability area also showed an initial expansion followed by contraction. The low-suitability area was expected to remain larger during 2061–2080 than in the current period (711,200 km2 vs. 679,100 km2). In contrast, under the SSP370 scenario, the high-suitability area was subjected to undergo an initial expansion followed by contraction over time and would decrease to only 269,500 km2 by 2061–2080. Concurrently, the moderate-suitability area was subjected to gradually reduce and the low-suitability area to progressively increased. A comparative analysis of the habitat area changes for S. glabra across different emission scenarios and time periods is shown in Fig. 7.Fig. 7
Area comparisons for different habitat suitability classes during various projected time periods for S. glabra.

sec.title: Centroid shifts in suitable habitats of S. glabra
sec.p:
The prediction results indicate differences in the centroid shift of suitable habitats for the S. glabra Roxb under varying climatic conditions (Fig. 8). Under the current climatic conditions, the optimal location was situated southeast of Guizhou Province and northeast of Miao and Dong Autonomous Prefecture, Guizhou Province (109.13°E, 26.72°N). Under the SSP126 scenario, the centroid shifted 86.9137 km northwestward (108.27°E, 26.83°N) in the 2041–2060 period and 93.3838 km southeastward (109.03°E, 26.35°N) in the 2061–2080 period. Despite these shifts, the centroid remained within the Qiandongnan Miao and Dong Autonomous Prefecture during both future periods under SSP126. According to the SSP370 scenario, the centroid shifted 96.5104 km westward in the 2041–2060 period but remained within Qiandongnan Miao and Dong Autonomous Prefecture (108.34°E, 26.67°N). However, in the 2061–2080 period, the centroid shifted southwestward into Qiannan Buyi and Miao Autonomous Prefecture (107.55°E, 26.09°N) and covered 103.5123 km. Collectively, these shifts suggest a southward migration trend in the centroid for the suitable habitats of S. glabra. The results of the Monte Carlo permutation test (Supplementary Table S2) indicate that the southward shift in the centroid of the suitable habitat for S. glabra exhibits extremely high statistical significance (p < 0.001) under all four future climate scenarios.Fig. 8
Spatial–temporal shifts in habitat suitability for S. glabra across the projected climate scenarios.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Biodiversity is essential for maintaining the health and stability of Earth’s ecosystems. However, multiple stressors, including climate change, environmental pollution, habitat destruction, and the overexploitation of natural resources are accelerating the loss in global biodiversity40,41. Therefore, predicting future distribution trends of species under climate change is critical for effective conservation of biodiversity. These predictions enhance our understanding of species adaptability and enable the implementation of appropriate conservation measures42. Smilax glabra is a valuable traditional Chinese medicinal herb with significant market demand because of a wide range of pharmacological activities. Therefore, predicting its future growth and distribution under changing environmental conditions is essential for safeguarding its wild germplasm resources.

sec.title: Ecological explanation of dominant environmental factors
sec.p: According to the MaxEnt model results, precipitation is the dominant environmental factor influencing the growth and distribution of S. glabra under current climatic conditions. Specifically, precipitation in November, May–June, and during the wettest quarter contributed most significantly. This pattern is likely linked to the species’ key phenological stages and physiological requirements. These three periods coincide with the flowering and fruiting phases of S. glabra4. Although specific pheno-physiological studies on S. glabra are limited, evidence from congeneric species and general ecological principles provides support. Research shows that water availability during flowering in many similar plants directly affects pollen viability, pollination success, and fruit set43–46. Several studies have reported that adequate rainfall enhances the content of bioactive compounds in medicinal plants, thereby improving herbs quality47–49. Therefore, the importance of precipitation from May to November highlighted by the model likely reflects this species’ strong reliance on moisture during its critical stages of vegetative and reproductive growth. While standard bioclimatic variables can reflect overall moisture patterns, they may fail to capture finer-scale seasonal moisture stress or optimal moisture windows critical for species survival and reproduction. However, monthly variables may lead to overfitting, particularly when species occurrence records are limited50. Therefore, we implemented rigorous screening to remove highly correlated redundant variables. Furthermore, temperature variables such as the mean diurnal range also contributed significantly, which aligns with the ecological preference of S. glabra for warm and humid conditions, as it is typically found on gentle slopes or in valley areas where cold air does not readily accumulate51. Concurrently, research on subtropical plant phenology indicates that both spring and autumn phenological events are strongly governed by precipitation and temperature52. Soil is another critical factor that influences plant growth because it provides essential mineral nutrients, water, air, and microbial communities. Soil also acts as a dynamic interface for material and energy exchange within ecosystems, thereby directly impacting plant growth and development53. In this study, clay content influenced the distribution of S. glabra. This finding aligns with records from the Traditional Chinese Medicine Network (https://www.zhzyw.com/), which shows that S. glabra is cultivated in sandy loam or clay loam soils.

It is noteworthy that the effects of climatic factors on species are not independent. Studies have revealed a significant interaction between temperature and precipitation: the effect of warming on advancing flowering is more pronounced under moist conditions, while the effect of increased precipitation on delaying flowering is more significant in colder environments54. This indicates that synergistic or antagonistic effects of hydrothermal combinations jointly determine the ultimate phenological expression. Although this study did not directly incorporate interaction terms into the model, the dominant factors identified suggest the central role of water availability. In the future, incorporating interaction terms between temperature and precipitation in the model may more precisely delineate the multidimensional boundaries of Smilax glabra’s ecological niche. Such interactions would be particularly critical when assessing the impacts of future extreme climatic events.

sec.title: Ecological implications of future distribution changes
sec.p: Currently, the suitable habitat of S. glabra is in the provinces south of the Yangtze River Basin in China. This distribution aligns well with its actual range55 and demonstrates reliability of the model. Future habitat predictions under the SSP126 scenario indicated that both the total and high-suitability habitat areas are projected to increase for S. glabra. This suggests that its current distribution has not yet reached its maximum potential and will continue to expand in the future. In the SSP370 scenario, while the overall expansion trend is expected to continue, the total suitable area is projected to decreases from the 2041–2060 period to the 2061–2080 period. The projected reduction in the high-suitability area suggests that climatic conditions are expected to become less favorable for S. glabra growth during the latter period.

Climate warming is anticipated to drive poleward (towards higher latitudes) migration for many plant species56. However, soil properties change along latitudinal gradients57. Therefore, soil in higher latitudes within study areas will be rendered unsuitable for many species. Consequently, some species might migrate towards lower latitudes because of climate warming58,59. Therefore, future conservation strategies should not only focus on the traditional "northern boundaries," but also place greater emphasis on preserving the integrity of core suitable habitats. Additionally, newly emerging suitable areas in the south should be incorporated into dynamic monitoring and conservation network planning.

A fundamental premise of this study, and of most species distribution models (SDMs), is that species distributions are limited solely by natural factors such as climate, topography, and soil, and that habitats are continuous and freely accessible. However, in reality, intensive human activities have profoundly altered landscapes and ecological processes. For an understory medicinal plant like Smilax glabra, which holds significant economic value, land-use change and habitat degradation represent threats to its actual distribution that are more immediate and decisive than future climate change. The MaxEnt model predicts the "climatically potential suitable habitat" in the absence of anthropogenic interference, whereas the "realizable suitable habitat" that a species can actually occupy is typically much smaller. With economic development, the conversion of forests to cropland, tea plantations, commercial plantations, or construction land directly destroys its living environment. Even if the future climate becomes more favorable, the loss of original forest habitats prevents S. glabra populations from recolonizing or expanding. Habitat fragmentation further hinders seed dispersal and gene flow, increasing the extinction risk for small, isolated populations. Over-harvesting of wild S. glabra resources driven by market demand is another major cause of population decline, potentially leading to local extinctions even within climatically suitable areas. Predicted expansions of suitable habitat, if located in regions of intense human activity, are unlikely to support viable populations due to persistent harvesting pressure. Therefore, the predictions presented here should be interpreted as the “climatically potential suitable habitat” under the assumption of intact habitat and the absence of anthropogenic pressure.

sec.title: Limitations and future prospects
sec.p: First, although the 184 distribution points used in this study were processed, their spatial density remains insufficient for covering the entire terrestrial area of China. This may affect the precise delineation of the species’ ecological niche boundaries, particularly in data-scarce marginal regions. Although rigorous variable screening was conducted to avoid multicollinearity, future studies could incorporate the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) for a more comprehensive multicollinearity assessment.

Secondly, the MaxEnt model is fundamentally a static, correlation-based model that fails to account for species dispersal capacity, interspecific competition, and critical anthropogenic disturbance factors. Beyond natural factors, human activities can profoundly influence species distribution and growth. In reality, intensive human activity may cause the actual distribution to be far smaller than the predicted range. While the model demonstrated robust internal validation performance, the absolute accuracy of the predictions in real-world geographical space remains to be further confirmed through field surveys, due to the lack of a large-scale, fully independent distribution dataset for external validation. Additionally, although multiple metrics were used to evaluate model performance, a limitation of this model is the lack of systematic optimization of key parameters such as the regularization multiplier and feature‑class combinations. Future studies could employ tools like ENMeval for parameter tuning to further validate and refine the prediction results.

Finally, this study relies on future climate projections from a single global climate model (GCM), BCC-CSM2-MR. Although this model offers higher resolution in both atmospheric and land‑surface processes, provides finer topographic representation, and demonstrates better performance in simulating orographic precipitation and local temperature distribution60, differences exist among GCMs. Using a single model does not allow quantification of the uncertainty inherent in climate projections themselves. This may introduce some bias in estimating changes in suitable habitat area. Future research could employ multiple GCMs to capture inter‑model variability.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This study employed a geographic information system software (ArcMap) and the ecological niche model (MaxEnt) to perform integrated analysis of climatic, precipitation, soil, and topographic variables with the occurrence data of Smilax glabra Roxb., to predict its current potential suitable habitat distribution across China. Furthermore, we predicted the potential suitable habitat extent, area, and spatiotemporal dynamics for S. glabra under two greenhouse gas emission scenarios (SSP126 and SSP370) for two future periods (2041–2060 and 2061–2080) within China.

Our findings demonstrate that precipitation, temperature, and soil are key environmental variables influencing the distribution and growth of S. glabra. Currently, the suitable habitat for S. glabra within China is primarily concentrated in the provinces south of the Yangtze River. Future projections indicate that the suitable habitat range will remain in the provinces south of the Yangtze. However, in the higher-emission SSP370 scenario, the area of high-suitability habitat is projected to decrease significantly. Furthermore, the centroid of the suitable habitat is projected to shift southwards, thereby indicating a migration trend of S. glabra towards lower latitudes. This study provides essential data for the conservation and sustainable utilization of S. glabra germplasm resources and offers valuable references for subsequent research.
